NUCLEAR REGULATORY COMMISSION

[Docket No. 70-07045; NRC-2026-4951]

Radiant Industries, Inc.; Special Nuclear Materials License 
Application for a Fuel Packing Facility; Environmental Assessment and 
Finding of No Significant Impact

AGENCY: Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

ACTION: Notice; issuance.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY: The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) is issuing a 
finding of no significant impact (FONSI) and accompanying environmental 
assessment (EA) regarding the NRC's consideration of a license 
application from Radiant Industries, Inc. (Radiant). Radiant is 
requesting a special nuclear material license for a facility in Oak 
Ridge, Tennessee. If granted, the license would allow Radiant to 
receive tri-structural isotropic (TRISO) particle fuel for fueling the 
Kaleidos self-contained, 1-megawatt electric reactors. This phase of 
the planned operational activities would only include packaging TRISO 
compacts into monoliths. Based on the EA, the NRC staff has concluded 
that there will be no significant impacts to environmental resources 
from the requested license, and therefore, a FONSI is appropriate.

DATES: The EA and FONSI referenced in this document are available on 
November 23, 2026.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

I. Introduction

    The NRC is considering issuing a special nuclear material license 
for a facility in Oak Ridge, Tennessee. Radiant is seeking a license 
under part 70 of title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR), 
``Domestic Licensing of Special Nuclear Material.'' The license would 
allow Radiant to

[[Page 75570]]

receive TRISO for fueling the Kaleidos self-contained, 1-megawatt 
electric reactors. As required by 10 CFR part 51, ``Environmental 
Protection Regulations for Domestic Licensing and Related Regulatory 
Functions,'' the NRC prepared an EA. Based on the results of the EA, 
the NRC has determined not to prepare an environmental impact statement 
(EIS) for the license application and is issuing a FONSI.
    A special nuclear material license would allow Radiant to receive, 
store, and load fresh fuel into fuel monoliths at a designated area of 
the project site. Site operation for future activities could include 
fresh fuel storage; reactor fueling, testing, refueling, and staging; 
and spent fuel storage. However, the proposed licensing action is 
limited to fresh fuel receipt and storage and loading TRISO compacts 
into monoliths.
    On May 1, 2026, the NRC notified Radiant by letter of its 
acceptance and docketing of Radiant's application that included an 
environmental report. The acceptance letter included observations of 
the application. On June 12, 2026, Radiant responded to the NRC's 
observations. The NRC staff issued a request for additional information 
(RAI) for the environmental review on June 24, 2026. Radiant responded 
to the RAI by letter dated June 29, 2026. Radiant also updated the 
application's environmental report.

II. Environmental Assessment

Description of the Proposed Action

    The NRC's proposed action is the issuance of a special nuclear 
material license to Radiant for a facility in Oak Ridge, Tennessee. NRC 
would issue the license under 10 CFR part 70 for the project, locally 
known as the R-50 Site in the city of Oak Ridge, Roane County, 
Tennessee. If granted, the license would allow Radiant to receive TRISO 
fuel for the Kaleidos self-contained 1-megawatt electric reactors. This 
phase of the planned operational activities is limited to fresh fuel 
receipt and storage, loading TRISO compacts into monoliths, and 
staging. Potential later phases may include reactor fueling, testing, 
and storage prior to deployment to potential customer sites. Additional 
activities must be licensed separately and may require environmental 
reviews.
    The location for the proposed action was selected by Radiant 
following an evaluation of several potential domestic locations and a 
subsequent screening process. The Oak Ridge property selection was 
based on several factors, which included the following: engaging with 
States and municipalities with the regulatory structure and interest in 
the nuclear industry; favorable site features that would reduce the 
environmental impacts of the proposed action; favorable site features 
that would reduce potential risks from accident scenarios due to 
natural conditions (seismic, flooding, wildfire); utility availability 
and transportation accessibility; and, availability of employees and 
community resources to support those employees.

Purpose and Need for the Proposed Action

    The purpose of and need for the proposed agency action--issuance of 
a special nuclear material license--is to allow Radiant to receive 
TRISO fuel to the project site and then construct and store fuel 
monoliths that can be used in small modular reactors. Small modular 
reactors are an excellent source of electric generation for sites that 
would benefit from a self-contained reactor due to location, lack of 
supporting infrastructure and the difficulty of developing conventional 
electrical generation. Radiant's goal is to develop the site and obtain 
additional authority, through licensing requests, to mass-produce self-
contained nuclear reactors for electrical generation using its own 
Kaleidos technology. There is a strong demand for small modular reactor 
technology at remote locations such as Arctic communities, defense 
installations and remote mining operations. This technology would 
provide those communities with dependable and sustainable power.

Environmental Impacts of the Proposed Action

    The NRC staff considered the potential impacts of the proposed 
action on land use; visual and scenic resources; climatology, 
meteorology, and air quality; noise; geology and soils; water 
resources; ecological resources; historic and cultural resources; 
socioeconomics; public and occupational health; transportation; and 
waste management.
    The NRC staff determined that the proposed action would result in 
limited environmental impacts. Construction activities, including 
grading, excavation, building construction, and installation of 
supporting infrastructure, would result in localized and temporary 
increases in noise, air emissions, traffic, and soil disturbance. 
Construction would occur primarily on previously disturbed industrial 
land, and applicable permitting requirements, erosion and sediment 
controls, stormwater management measures, and other best management 
practices would minimize potential impacts. Operational activities 
would occur primarily within enclosed industrial facilities and would 
involve receipt, storage, handling, and packaging of fresh TRISO fuel. 
The NRC staff does not expect these activities to result in significant 
impacts to land use, visual resources, air quality, noise, geology and 
soils, or transportation.
    The proposed action would not require groundwater withdrawals or 
direct discharges to surface waters. Potential effects on water 
resources would primarily involve erosion and sediment transport during 
construction and would be minimized through implementation of 
applicable stormwater management and erosion-control measures. 
Ecological impacts would primarily consist of limited habitat loss, 
including clearing approximately 0.6 acres of trees, and temporary 
noise-related disturbance to wildlife. The NRC staff determined that 
impacts to ecological resources would be small, based on the previously 
disturbed nature of the site, the limited construction footprint, and 
avoidance of wetland and riparian areas. The NRC staff also considered 
Federally protected species and habitats in its environmental review 
and conducted consultation under Section 7 of the Endangered Species 
Act.
    The NRC staff evaluated potential impacts to historic and cultural 
resources in coordination with the Tennessee State Historic 
Preservation Officer (TN SHPO), the National Park Service, the U.S. 
Department of Energy (DOE), and Federally recognized Indian Tribes. The 
TN SHPO concurred with the NRC staff's determination of no adverse 
effect. The proposed action is also expected to result in limited 
socioeconomic and transportation effects associated with construction 
employment, routine facility operations, and the movement of workers 
and materials. These activities would occur within an established 
industrial area with existing transportation infrastructure and 
available regional services.
    Potential public and occupational health impacts would be minimized 
through engineered facility controls, administrative procedures, 
radiation protection programs, and compliance with applicable Federal, 
State, and local requirements. The NRC staff separately evaluated 
radiological impacts and postulated accidents associated with the 
proposed activities. Waste generated during construction and operation 
would include conventional construction debris, routine operational 
waste, and potentially small quantities of radioactive waste associated 
with fuel

[[Page 75571]]

handling and maintenance. These materials would be appropriately 
characterized, managed, and transferred to authorized recycling, 
treatment, or disposal facilities, as applicable.

Environmental Impacts of the Alternatives to the Proposed Action

    As an alternative to the proposed action, the NRC staff considered 
the ``no-action alternative.'' Under the no-action alternative, the NRC 
would not issue a license to Radiant because regulatory requirements 
have not been met. Consequently, the facility would not be built and 
production of the fuel monoliths needed for small modular reactors 
would not be available to the market. Remote industrial activities, 
small communities, emergency operations and military installations 
would continue existing operations depending on diesel fuel for 
electricity. If the project is not built at the R-50 Site, the 
environment would remain the same.

Agencies and Persons Consulted

    The NRC submitted the draft EA to the State Liaison Officer at the 
Tennessee Department of Radiological Health (Department) for their 
review and comment on October 1, 2026. The Department responded on 
October 19, 2026, with no comments. National Historic Preservation Act 
(NHPA) consultation was conducted pursuant to 36 CFR 800.8(c). The NRC 
staff initiated consultation with 18 Federally recognized Indian Tribes 
with potential historic and ancestral ties to the project vicinity: (1) 
Absentee Shawnee Tribe, (2) Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas, (3) 
Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town, (4) Cherokee Nation, (5) Chickasaw 
Nation, (6) Coushatta Tribe of Louisiana, (7) Delaware Nation, (8) 
Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians, (9) Eastern Shawnee Tribe of 
Oklahoma, (10) Jena Band of Choctaw Indians, (11) Kialegee Tribal Town, 
(12) Muscogee Nation, (13) Poarch Band of Creek Indians, (14) Seminole 
Nation of Oklahoma, (15) Seminole Tribe of Florida, (16) Shawnee Tribe, 
(17) Thlopthlocco Tribal Town, and (18) United Keetoowah Band of 
Cherokee Indians. These consultations were conducted to make sure the 
Tribes were afforded an opportunity to identify their concerns, provide 
advice on the identification and evaluation of historic properties, 
including those of traditional religious and cultural importance, and, 
if necessary, participate in the resolution of any adverse effects to 
such properties. The Muscogee Nation responded with a request for 
additional information that was subsequently provided by the NRC staff. 
The Chickasaw Nation responded that the project was located outside 
their area of interest. The Shawnee Tribe responded that they are not 
aware of any cultural resources that would be negatively impacted by 
the project and asked to be updated on the project.
    The NRC staff also initiated consultation with the TN SHPO, 
National Park Service, and DOE, and informed the Advisory Council on 
Historic Preservation of its intent to use the National Environmental 
Policy Act process to satisfy NRC's Section 106 responsibilities 
pursuant to paragraph 800.8(c) of title 36 of the Code of Federal 
Regulations (36 CFR) (all consulting parties were similarly notified). 
The TN SHPO responded stating that no archaeological resources would be 
affected and that there would be no adverse effect to the Manhattan 
Project National Historic Park. The DOE responded stating that they do 
not need to participate in consultation. The Advisory Council responded 
reminding the NRC staff of responsibilities pursuant to 36 CFR 
800.8(c). The National Park Service responded that they have no 
comments at this time and requested confirmation that the NRC staff are 
conducting Tribal consultations.
    Subsequently, the NRC staff's determination of no adverse effect 
and the draft historic and cultural resources section of the EA was 
made publicly available and available to the TN SHPO, the National Park 
Service, and 18 Federally recognized Tribes. Responses were received 
from the Shawnee Tribe; request to be informed if there is a discovery 
situation) and the Delaware Nation; declining to participate in 
consultation). Also, the TN SHPO responded with their concurrence on 
the NRC staff's finding of no adverse effect.
    On August 28, 2026, the NRC staff accessed the U.S. Fish and 
Wildlife Service (FWS) Information for Planning and Consultation system 
and obtained a species list for the proposed action area. The review 
identified Federally listed species and/or other species of 
conservation concern with the potential to occur within the action 
area. NRC staff used the Tennessee Determination Key to analyze the 
impacts to gray bat (Myotis grisescens), spotfin chub (Erimonax 
monachus), Virginia spiraea (Spiraea virginiana), White fringeless 
orchid (Platanthera integrilabia) and the species-specific 
determination keys to analyze the impacts to the tricolored bat 
(Perimyotis subflavus) and the Indiana bat (Myotis sodalis). Based on 
the NRC staff's answers and the assistance of the Tennessee 
determination key, NRC determined that the impacts to all six species 
would be ``Not Likely to Adversely Affect (NLAA).''
    For species listed above with a determination of ``Not Likely to 
Adversely Affect (NLAA),'' no further action is necessary, unless the 
FWS contacts the NRC within 30 calendar days to clarify details of the 
action or request additional information. The 30-day review period 
ended on September 27, 2026, and the NRC staff received no comments 
from the FWS.

III. Finding of No Significant Impact

    Based on its review of the special nuclear material license 
request, in accordance with the requirements of 10 CFR part 51, the NRC 
staff has determined that issuing the requested license would not 
significantly affect the quality of the human environment. No 
significant radiological or non-radiological impacts are expected from 
the proposed action. Therefore, the NRC staff has determined that 
pursuant to 10 CFR 51.31, ``Determinations based on environmental 
assessment,'' preparation of an EIS is not required for the proposed 
action, and pursuant to 10 CFR 51.32, ``Finding of no significant 
impact,'' a FONSI is appropriate. In accordance with 10 CFR 
51.32(a)(4), this FONSI incorporates the EA set forth in this notice by 
reference.
